# My grooming van nearly caught fire. Here’s what I wish I’d checked.

Last Wednesday, October 28, at around 2:15 in the afternoon, I was in a client’s driveway in Bedford drying a Bernese mountain dog named Moose.

The dryer was on high. Moose was being Moose. Everything felt normal until I smelled hot plastic.

At first I thought it was the dryer motor. Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat where my batteries are.

I killed the battery switch, got Moose out through the side door, and used the extinguisher a bit. I’m still not even sure whether I needed to use it, but I wasn’t going to stand there trying to work that out with smoke coming from the battery compartment.

Moose was still damp. He was thrilled, honestly.

His mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook. I keep thinking about how kind that was, and how differently the afternoon could have gone.

Everyone is okay. Moose is okay. But a cable and connection in my van’s electrical system got hot enough to melt, and I’m now looking at a minimum of three weeks off the road.

I’m writing this partly because Tasha is about to put down a deposit with the same builder who did my van, and partly because I know a lot of other mobile groomers read this. I trusted my build because it looked tidy. I have learned the hard way that **tidy is not the same as right**.

Before I go any further: **I’m a dog groomer, not an electrician.** I’m sharing what happened, what the electrician showed me, and the notes I took afterward. This is not a guide to installing or repairing a van electrical system. If anything about yours worries you, turn it off and get a qualified professional to look at it.

## What’s in my van

My van was built by Darren at Coastline Van Fitouts in spring 2025. It has a 3,000-watt inverter and two 200 amp-hour lithium batteries in a 12-volt setup.

For anyone who, like me, mostly just wanted to plug in a dryer and get on with the dogs: the inverter takes power from the batteries and turns it into the kind of power used by equipment like the dryer. The cables between the batteries and inverter have to carry a lot of current when the equipment is running.

My dryer pulls approximately 1,800 to 2,000 watts on high. The water heater sometimes runs too, depending on what else is happening.

After the incident, Priya from Sackville Marine Electric came to look at the damage. The cable from the battery to the inverter was **4 AWG**. Priya told me it should have been **2/0 AWG** for the 3,000-watt inverter at 12 volts.

Those numbers are cable sizes. Annoyingly, they don’t work the way my brain expects: 2/0 is substantially thicker than 4 AWG. The size needed in a particular van depends on more than the inverter’s advertised wattage, including cable length, installation conditions and the equipment specifications. That’s a job for the person designing and checking the system, not something to guess from a blog post.

## Why so much current?

This was the part I had to ask Priya about more than once.

A rough starting point is watts divided by volts. At 12 volts, 1,800 watts works out to 150 amps, and 2,000 watts works out to about 167 amps.

But that simple calculation doesn’t include inverter losses. The batteries can also be above or below exactly 12 volts while operating, and any other equipment running adds to the load. So the actual battery-side current while the dryer is running can be higher than those first numbers. With other loads, it could reach or exceed 250 amps depending on what’s running and how the system is set up.

That is a lot of current going through a cable and its connections. It’s also why “it’s only 12 volts” does **not** mean there’s nothing to worry about.

For scale, the same rough division for the inverter’s full 3,000-watt output is 250 amps at 12 volts, before accounting for inverter losses. I don’t know exactly what the current was at the moment my cable overheated. I didn’t have a measurement, and I don’t want to pretend I did. But it’s clear that a grooming van can place a very heavy demand on its battery cables.

Also, the 200 amp-hour figure on each of my batteries describes capacity, not a promise that any cable connected to them can safely carry 200 amps. That distinction was news to me.

## What Priya found

The damage was at the positive end of the cable. The lug—the metal end fitting that connects the cable to a terminal—was black, and the cable jacket had melted back about three centimetres.

Priya told me the lug appeared to have been crimped with something like pliers or a hammer rather than a proper crimper. Heat-shrink had been covering it, so it wasn’t something I’d noticed just by looking at the setup.

A bad connection can create resistance, and resistance under a high current can produce heat. From what Priya showed me, the undersized cable and the poor-looking crimp were serious concerns. I can’t tell you exactly how much each contributed or give you a full engineering report on the failure. What I can tell you is that the connection got hot enough to blacken and melt the surrounding cable jacket, and Priya said the main runs need to be rewired.

The fuse also raised a concern. Mine was a **300-amp ANL fuse**, mounted roughly **90 centimetres from the battery**. Priya said it should have been within about **18 centimetres**. The reason that distance matters, as she explained it to me, is that the stretch of cable between a battery and its fuse can be left unprotected by that fuse.

The exact fuse type, rating and placement need to be selected for the whole system and the applicable requirements. A fuse isn’t just a number you match to the biggest thing in the van, and moving one closer to the battery isn’t a DIY fix for an undersized cable or a bad connection. Please get a professional to assess all of it together.

Priya also pulled up my damage photos next to thermal camera shots of her own van running a similar kind of load. Hers barely got warm. The difference was wild. That comparison really brought home to me that this wasn’t something I should just chalk up to “big dryer, things get hot.”

And one more thing I hadn’t thought enough about: there was no smoke detector in the back of my van. There was only the one in the cab that came with it. I’m going to discuss appropriate detection and placement for the grooming and battery areas as part of the repair.

## A note about the builder

I’m naming Coastline Van Fitouts and Darren because Tasha is considering a deposit with the same builder, and I think the details matter to other groomers making that decision.

I’m not trying to trash anyone. I’m describing my own setup, what happened, and what Priya told me after inspecting it. I’ve sent Darren three texts and an email and haven’t had an answer so far. If that changes, I’ll include an update when I have one.

I also want to be fair about what I don’t know. I don’t know the exact current at the time of the incident, and I’m not claiming that every van from this builder has the same issue. If you have one, that doesn’t mean yours is unsafe—but I do think an independent inspection is worth considering, especially if you don’t have the electrical specifications for your build.

## Tasha: before you pay a deposit

I know we’ve already talked, but I’m putting this here for anyone else at the same stage.

Ask the builder for the electrical specifications **in writing before you pay**. Not just “it’ll handle a dryer” or “we do these all the time.” Ask for enough detail that an independent qualified electrician can review the proposed setup for the equipment you actually intend to use.

I’d ask for:

- The inverter’s make, model and continuous power rating.
- The battery make, model, capacity and voltage, and how the batteries will be connected.
- The size and approximate length of the main battery-to-inverter cables.
- The fuse type, rating and planned location for those main cables.
- How the cable ends will be terminated and what equipment will be used to crimp them.
- A list of the loads the system is designed to run, including whether the dryer and water heater can run at the same time.
- The planned battery isolation switch and how you’re supposed to shut the system down in an emergency.
- The plan for smoke detection, an accessible extinguisher and battery installation.
- A wiring diagram and the equipment manuals you’ll receive with the finished van.
- Who will inspect or verify the completed electrical installation.

Then tell them the actual equipment you use, not just “grooming equipment.” Give them the dryer’s rated wattage and the water heater details, and be honest about what you might have on at the same time.

I would also pay an independent qualified professional to review the plan before handing over the deposit. That’s not because every builder is doing something wrong. It’s because most of us are paying for a working van, not training to judge high-current wiring ourselves.

## A power-off checklist for your own van

This is meant to help you notice questions or warning signs, **not** to prove your van is safe. A connection can look fine from the outside and still need professional attention.

Before looking, shut down your equipment and switch off the electrical system using the controls you’ve been instructed to use. **Do not disconnect battery cables, remove covers, open fuse holders, peel back heat-shrink, touch terminals or move wiring.** Switching off an inverter or battery switch does not necessarily make every cable or terminal safe; batteries can still energize parts of the system.

If anything is hot, smoking, hissing, smells strongly of burning, or looks actively damaged, don’t investigate it yourself. Get people and animals away, call 911 if there’s smoke or fire, and follow emergency responders’ instructions.

When everything is cool and there’s no immediate danger, here are things you can check without touching the wiring:

### 1. Find your paperwork

Do you have a wiring diagram, equipment manuals and a list of cable and fuse specifications? If not, ask your builder for them.

Write down the inverter and battery models, as well as the rated power of your dryer and other major equipment. A professional can use that information when reviewing the system.

### 2. Look for obvious damage from a safe distance

Without opening anything or moving cables, can you see melted or discoloured insulation, scorch marks, damaged cable covering, or a connection that looks blackened?

Have you noticed a recurring hot-plastic or electrical smell? Don’t dismiss it because the equipment still works. Stop using the system and have it checked.

### 3. Know where the shutoffs are

Can you find the battery isolation switch quickly? Do you know what it actually shuts off? Ask your builder or electrician to show you, and make sure anyone who works in the van knows too.

Remember that even after a switch is turned off, some parts may remain live.

### 4. Check your smoke detection and extinguisher plan

Where are your detectors? Can you hear an alarm from where you work? Is your extinguisher accessible without reaching past the batteries or a possible fire?

Check the equipment instructions and ask a qualified professional what detection and fire-protection arrangements are appropriate for your van. Also make sure you know how to get yourself, the dog and anyone else out quickly. Equipment can be replaced; you and the dog can’t.

### 5. Ask for an independent inspection

If you don’t know your cable sizes, fuse specifications or installation details—or if anything looks or smells wrong—book a qualified electrician who is experienced with this kind of high-current vehicle electrical system.

Ask them to assess the cables, connections, fuses, protection, battery installation and loads as a complete system. Don’t assume that matching my numbers will make your setup safe.

## About infrared thermometers

I bought a cheap infrared thermometer for about $40 at Canadian Tire after this happened. I think it’s a useful thing to have, but I want to be clear about its limits.

An infrared thermometer measures the surface it’s pointed at, and readings can be misleading on shiny metal or if the spot being measured is smaller than the area the thermometer sees. It also won’t necessarily reveal a hot spot hidden under heat-shrink, inside a connection or behind a cover. A normal reading is **not** proof that wiring is safe.

Please don’t open an energized compartment or reach around live terminals to take measurements. If you want temperature checks under load, ask a qualified professional how they should be done safely. Priya’s thermal camera comparison was useful because she knew what she was looking at and how to check it.

## Where things stand

The repair quote is **$4,200** for rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and a Class T fuse. Parts are on order, and I’ve been told **at least three weeks**.

I’ve cancelled 31 appointments so far. Insurance has said maybe; the adjuster is coming Thursday.

I’m trying to stay practical and make the calls I need to make, but I’d be lying if I said I’m calm about it. That van is my whole income. Rent is due on the first, and right now I don’t know exactly what insurance will cover or when I’ll be back working.

Mostly, though, I keep coming back to how lucky we were. I smelled something, I saw the smoke, and I got Moose out. His mom sat with me while I tried to stop shaking. It could have been so much worse.

If you take one thing from this, please don’t let a clean-looking installation be the only reassurance you have. Get the details, ask questions and have someone qualified check the system—especially before you put down a deposit or if anything smells hot.

I’ll post another update when the van is back and I know more. In the meantime, thank you to everyone who’s been patient about appointments, and to Moose’s mom for the coffee. Moose, I hope you enjoyed your slightly damp afternoon off.
